(CNN) -- U.S. health officials said Wednesday they have found a contaminant in a blood-thinning drug produced by Baxter Healthcare Corp. that has been linked to more than a dozen deaths in the United States. The drug can keep potentially life-threatening blood clots from forming in the veins, arteries, and lungs. In early February, the Food and Drug Administration launched an investigation and then a recall of some forms of the product. The scrutiny began after a spike in reports of health problems associated with heparin, a drug made by Baxter from pig intestines at plants in China and Wisconsin. Though the cause of the problems has not been determined, FDA investigators found "a heparin-like compound -- that is not heparin -- present in some of the active pharmaceutical ingredients" in both facilities, said Dr. Janet Woodcock, acting director of the FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research. The contaminant, which made up 5 percent to 20 percent of each sample tested, "reacts like heparin in some of the conventional tests used for heparin," which explains why it was not picked up, she told reporters in a conference call. No causal link between the contaminant and the adverse events has been established yet, Woodcock said. She added that it was not clear whether the contaminant was added accidentally, as part of the processing or deliberately. It also was not clear whether the contaminant was introduced in the company's plant in Wisconsin or the one in China, Woodcock said. Though she said the exact structure of the contaminant has not been identified, "it is similar to heparin glycans." Glycans are polysaccharides, a complex class of carbohydrate. She added it was unclear whether other heparin products used outside the United States might also contain the product. Later this week, the agency will release recommendations on how manufacturers and regulators can screen for the contaminant, she said. Last year, pet food made in China was found to be tainted with an ingredient that replaced more expensive protein and that initial tests did not identify as a contaminant. Asked if the heparin contamination could be a similar case, Woodcock said, "It's possible." Doctors have used the blood-thinner for 60 years with "no history of any problems whatsoever," said the FDA commissioner, Dr. Andrew C. von Eschenbach. Its intravenous use can keep potentially life-threatening blood clots from forming in the veins, arteries and lungs. Von Eschenbach said it would be "disingenuous" to expect the agency would be able to inspect "every institution in every case." Over the last fiscal year, the agency reported having inspected more than 1,000 foreign plants, a record. Since the agency issued its report that 19 deaths had been linked to the drug since January 1, 2007, it has received word of another 27 deaths, "but many of those do not fit our definition of this type of event," Woodcock said. In all, the FDA has received 785 heparin-linked reports of adverse events -- including difficulty breathing, nausea, vomiting, excessive sweating and plummeting blood pressure that can lead to life-threatening shock. "They're continuing to come in fairly rapidly because there has been a lot of reporting of this," she said. In a written statement, Baxter said its tests have suggested "that the root cause may be associated with the crude heparin, sourced from China, or from the subsequent processing of that product before it reaches Baxter." Meanwhile, Scientific Protein Laboratories LLC, which supplies the company with the active pharmaceutical ingredients, issued a statement saying it is working with the FDA, Baxter and outside experts to identify the cause of the adverse events. "Thus far, no conclusions have been reached about the root cause," it said. "It is premature to conclude that the heparin active pharmaceutical ingredient sourced from China and provided by SPL to Baxter is responsible for these adverse events." It said that its voluntary recall of suspect product was being made as a precaution.  E-mail to a friend .

(CNN) — U.S. health officials said Wednesday that they have identified a contaminant in a blood-thinning drug produced by Baxter Healthcare Corp. that has been linked to more than a dozen deaths in the United States.

The drug is used to help prevent potentially life-threatening blood clots from forming in the veins, arteries and lungs. In early February, the Food and Drug Administration launched an investigation and subsequently recalled certain forms of the product. The review began after a surge in reports of health problems associated with heparin, a drug manufactured by Baxter from pig intestines at facilities in China and Wisconsin.

Although the cause of the problems has not yet been determined, FDA investigators found “a heparin-like compound — that is not heparin — present in some of the active pharmaceutical ingredients” at both facilities, said Dr. Janet Woodcock, acting director of the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research.

The contaminant, which accounted for 5 percent to 20 percent of each sample tested, “reacts like heparin in some of the conventional tests used for heparin,” which explains why it was not detected earlier, Woodcock told reporters during a conference call.

Woodcock said no causal link has yet been established between the contaminant and the adverse events. She added that it remains unclear whether the contaminant was introduced accidentally, as part of the processing, or deliberately. It is also unclear whether the contaminant was introduced at the company’s Wisconsin facility or at its plant in China.

While the precise structure of the contaminant has not been identified, Woodcock said “it is similar to heparin glycans.” Glycans are polysaccharides, a complex class of carbohydrates. She added that it is unclear whether other heparin products used outside the United States might also contain the substance.

Later this week, the agency will release recommendations on how manufacturers and regulators can screen for the contaminant, she said.

Last year, pet food made in China was found to be tainted with an ingredient that replaced more expensive protein and was not identified as a contaminant by initial tests. Asked whether the heparin contamination could be a similar case, Woodcock said, “It’s possible.”

Doctors have used the blood thinner for 60 years with “no history of any problems whatsoever,” said FDA Commissioner Dr. Andrew C. von Eschenbach. Its intravenous use can prevent potentially life-threatening blood clots from forming in the veins, arteries and lungs.

Von Eschenbach said it would be “disingenuous” to expect the agency to be able to inspect “every institution in every case.” During the last fiscal year, the agency reported inspecting more than 1,000 foreign plants, a record number.

Since the agency reported that 19 deaths had been linked to the drug since January 1, 2007, it has received reports of another 27 deaths, “but many of those do not fit our definition of this type of event,” Woodcock said.

In total, the FDA has received 785 heparin-linked reports of adverse events, including difficulty breathing, nausea, vomiting, excessive sweating and sharply falling blood pressure that can lead to life-threatening shock.

“They’re continuing to come in fairly rapidly because there has been a lot of reporting of this,” Woodcock said.

In a written statement, Baxter said its tests have suggested “that the root cause may be associated with the crude heparin, sourced from China, or from the subsequent processing of that product before it reaches Baxter.”

Meanwhile, Scientific Protein Laboratories LLC, which supplies Baxter with the active pharmaceutical ingredients, issued a statement saying it is working with the FDA, Baxter and outside experts to identify the cause of the adverse events.

“Thus far, no conclusions have been reached about the root cause,” the statement said. “It is premature to conclude that the heparin active pharmaceutical ingredient sourced from China and provided by SPL to Baxter is responsible for these adverse events.”

The company said its voluntary recall of the suspect product was being conducted as a precaution.

U.S. health authorities announced Wednesday that they had detected an impurity in a blood-thinning medication manufactured by Baxter Healthcare Corp., a product that has been associated with more than a dozen deaths in the United States.

The medicine, heparin, is used to help prevent dangerous blood clots from developing in veins, arteries, and the lungs. In early February, the Food and Drug Administration began investigating the product and later recalled certain versions of it after reports of medical complications connected to Baxter’s heparin sharply increased.

Baxter makes the drug from pig intestines at facilities in China and Wisconsin. Although investigators have not yet identified what caused the reported reactions, FDA officials found “a heparin-like compound — that is not heparin” in some of the active pharmaceutical ingredients from both locations, according to Dr. Janet Woodcock, acting director of the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research.

Woodcock told reporters during a conference call that the impurity accounted for 5 percent to 20 percent of each sample examined. She said it “reacts like heparin in some of the conventional tests used for heparin,” which is why earlier testing failed to detect it.

She emphasized that officials have not yet proven that the contaminant caused the adverse reactions. It also remains unknown whether the substance entered the product unintentionally during manufacturing or was added on purpose. Investigators likewise have not determined whether the contamination originated at Baxter’s Wisconsin facility or at the plant in China.

Woodcock said the precise chemical structure of the contaminant has not been determined, but that it appears to be similar to heparin glycans. Glycans are polysaccharides, a complicated type of carbohydrate. She also said it was not known whether heparin products used in countries outside the United States could contain the same substance.

The FDA plans to issue guidance later this week explaining how manufacturers and regulators can test for the contaminant, Woodcock said.

The situation drew comparisons to the previous year’s discovery that pet food made in China had been adulterated with an ingredient used as a cheaper substitute for protein, which early tests had not identified as contamination. When asked whether the heparin issue could be similar, Woodcock replied, “It’s possible.”

FDA Commissioner Dr. Andrew C. von Eschenbach said physicians have relied on the blood thinner for 60 years with “no history of any problems whatsoever.” Administered intravenously, the drug helps prevent potentially fatal clots in veins, arteries, and lungs.

Von Eschenbach said it would be “disingenuous” to assume the FDA could examine “every institution in every case.” During the previous fiscal year, the agency said it had inspected more than 1,000 foreign manufacturing plants, the highest number it had ever recorded.

Since the FDA reported that 19 deaths had been linked to heparin since January 1, 2007, the agency has learned of 27 additional deaths, Woodcock said. However, she noted that “many of those do not fit our definition of this type of event.”

Overall, the FDA has received 785 reports of adverse events connected to heparin. Reported symptoms have included trouble breathing, nausea, vomiting, heavy sweating, and a sharp drop in blood pressure that can result in life-threatening shock.

“They’re continuing to come in fairly rapidly because there has been a lot of reporting of this,” Woodcock said.

In a written statement, Baxter said its own testing indicated “that the root cause may be associated with the crude heparin, sourced from China, or from the subsequent processing of that product before it reaches Baxter.”

Scientific Protein Laboratories LLC, which provides Baxter with the active pharmaceutical ingredients, also released a statement saying it is cooperating with the FDA, Baxter, and outside specialists to determine what caused the adverse events.

“Thus far, no conclusions have been reached about the root cause,” the company said. “It is premature to conclude that the heparin active pharmaceutical ingredient sourced from China and provided by SPL to Baxter is responsible for these adverse events.”

The company said it was voluntarily recalling the suspect product as a precaution.

counterfactuals.output:
**FDA finds heparin-like contaminant in Baxter blood thinner linked to deaths**

*By [Staff Writer]*

WASHINGTON (CNN) — Federal health officials said Wednesday they have identified a heparin-like contaminant in batches of Baxter Healthcare’s blood thinner heparin, a widely used drug that has been linked to severe allergic-type reactions and deaths in the United States.

The Food and Drug Administration said the contaminant, described as a chemically altered substance that closely resembles heparin, was found in the active pharmaceutical ingredient used to make Baxter’s injectable heparin products. Baxter recalled multiple heparin products after reports of patients suffering dangerous reactions, including sharp drops in blood pressure, difficulty breathing, nausea, vomiting and rapid swelling.

FDA officials said they were investigating whether the contaminant was connected to reports of deaths and hundreds of adverse events among patients who received the drug.

Dr. Janet Woodcock, director of the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, said the substance was difficult to detect because it behaved so much like heparin in routine testing.

“This contaminant is heparin-like,” Woodcock said. “It mimics heparin very closely.”

The agency said the suspect ingredient was traced through Baxter’s supply chain to a plant in China that produced crude heparin material, which was then processed before being used in finished products manufactured at Baxter’s facility in Wisconsin. FDA inspectors have been examining both the Chinese source and Baxter’s U.S. manufacturing operations as part of the investigation.

Heparin is made from pig intestines and is used in hospitals and clinics to prevent blood clots during kidney dialysis, heart surgery and other procedures. Because it is given to seriously ill patients, determining whether a death was caused by heparin or by an underlying condition can be difficult, officials said.

Still, the FDA said the pattern of reactions raised serious concerns. The agency received reports of hundreds of adverse events associated with heparin products, including deaths, after Baxter’s product was distributed.

FDA Commissioner Dr. Andrew von Eschenbach said the agency was working with Baxter, Chinese regulators and other international authorities to determine how the contaminant entered the supply chain.

“We are committed to finding out how this happened,” von Eschenbach said, adding that the FDA’s priority was protecting patients while maintaining access to a critical medication.

Baxter has said it is cooperating with federal investigators and has suspended production of the affected heparin products. The company’s Wisconsin plant was involved in producing finished doses, while the raw heparin material originated from suppliers tied to China, officials said.

The FDA said it has developed new testing methods to screen heparin supplies for the contaminant and has asked manufacturers to use those tests before releasing products to the market.

Woodcock said investigators had not yet determined whether the contamination was accidental or deliberate.

“We don’t know whether it was introduced intentionally or whether it was introduced by accident,” she said.

Health officials urged doctors to monitor patients closely and use alternative heparin products when appropriate, but they cautioned that heparin remains an essential drug for many life-saving procedures.

**BREAKING NEWS: Baxter Heparin Contamination Probe Expands to Chinese Supply Chain**

**WASHINGTON —** Federal investigators are intensifying their probe into contaminated batches of the blood thinner **heparin** sold by **Baxter International**, after a nationwide **FDA recall** and reports linking the product to severe allergic-type reactions, injuries, and deaths.

The **U.S. Food and Drug Administration** has said Baxter recalled heparin products after patients experienced sudden and sometimes life-threatening reactions, including difficulty breathing, nausea, vomiting, excessive sweating, and dangerous drops in blood pressure. The agency has been investigating whether a contaminant entered the drug through the complex global supply chain used to produce heparin, which is derived from pig intestines.

According to FDA reports from the investigation, the contaminated heparin has been associated with **dozens of deaths — including figures reported as high as 81 — and hundreds of adverse event reports, including roughly 785 serious reactions**. Officials have cautioned that adverse-event reports do not always prove a drug caused a death or injury, but the pattern triggered urgent scrutiny.

Investigators have focused in part on a **possible Chinese supply chain connection**. Baxter’s heparin active ingredient was supplied by **Scientific Protein Laboratories**, or **SPL**, which operated through a China-linked supply chain that included **Changzhou SPL**. FDA officials identified a contaminant, later described as an **oversulfated chondroitin sulfate–like substance**, in some heparin batches. The substance can mimic heparin in standard tests, raising concerns that it may have been deliberately or accidentally introduced before final manufacturing.

**Baxter** has said it moved quickly to recall affected heparin products and has cooperated fully with the FDA investigation. The company has emphasized that the contamination appears to have occurred before the active ingredient reached Baxter’s finished-drug manufacturing process.

**Scientific Protein Laboratories** has also said it is cooperating with regulators and investigating its supply chain. SPL has stated that it was working with authorities to determine how the contaminant entered the product stream and has defended its commitment to quality and safety standards.

The FDA says the case highlights the risks of increasingly global pharmaceutical supply chains, especially when raw materials pass through multiple brokers, workshops, or processing facilities before reaching a finished-drug manufacturer.

Federal officials continue to examine whether the contamination was economically motivated, accidental, or the result of inadequate supply chain controls.

**FDA finds unidentified contaminant in heparin linked to deaths, reactions**

**WASHINGTON (CNN) — Wednesday** — U.S. health officials said Wednesday they have found an unidentified contaminant in some supplies of the blood thinner heparin, a discovery that may help explain a wave of severe allergic-type reactions and deaths among patients who received the widely used drug.

The Food and Drug Administration said the contaminant was detected in heparin active pharmaceutical ingredients and finished products associated with recent adverse-event reports. Officials said the substance is not a normal component of heparin and appears to have chemical properties that may allow it to evade standard quality-control tests.

Heparin is commonly used in hospitals, dialysis centers and operating rooms to prevent blood clots. It is often given to patients undergoing kidney dialysis, heart surgery and other procedures where clotting can pose a serious risk.

Federal officials said patients have reported sudden drops in blood pressure, difficulty breathing, nausea, vomiting, sweating and other symptoms shortly after receiving certain heparin products. Some reactions were severe, and deaths have been reported, though investigators said they are still determining whether heparin was the direct cause in every case.

The FDA said it is working with manufacturers, state authorities and international regulators to trace the source of the contaminant and determine how it entered the supply chain. Much of the raw material used to make heparin comes from pig intestines and is processed through a global network of suppliers before reaching U.S. drugmakers.

Health officials said the affected products were being recalled or withheld from the market while testing continues. Hospitals and clinicians were urged to check their inventories, follow recall notices and report any suspected reactions.

The agency said alternative blood thinners are available for some patients, but warned that heparin remains medically necessary in many settings. Doctors should weigh the risks and benefits before changing treatment, officials said.

Investigators said the contaminant appears to be present in some batches but not others, raising questions about whether it was introduced accidentally during processing or deliberately added to the product. FDA officials said they had not reached a conclusion.

The discovery has intensified scrutiny of the pharmaceutical supply chain, particularly ingredients produced overseas and used in critical U.S. medicines. Lawmakers and patient-safety advocates have called for stronger inspections and more sophisticated testing of imported drug ingredients.

The FDA said it is developing improved screening methods to detect the contaminant and prevent additional tainted heparin from reaching patients.

---

## Contaminated blood thinner raises questions about global drug supply

A deadly contamination crisis involving the widely used blood thinner heparin has exposed serious weaknesses in the global pharmaceutical supply chain and raised troubling questions about whether the adulteration was accidental or deliberate.

In 2008, U.S. health officials investigated a surge of severe allergic-type reactions and deaths among patients given heparin, a drug commonly used during dialysis, heart surgery and other medical procedures to prevent blood clots. Much of the attention focused on products sold by Baxter Healthcare, one of the major suppliers of heparin in the United States.

Heparin is derived from pig intestines, and the raw material often moves through a complex chain of slaughterhouses, workshops, consolidators and processing plants before becoming an injectable medicine. In this case, investigators traced some of the drug ingredients to China, where oversight of the early stages of production was limited and difficult to verify.

The contaminant was later identified as oversulfated chondroitin sulfate, a chemically altered substance that can resemble heparin in standard quality tests but may trigger dangerous reactions in patients. Because it mimicked some of heparin’s properties, the contaminant was not detected by routine screening methods used at the time.

The Food and Drug Administration faced criticism after it emerged that an overseas facility connected to Baxter’s supply chain had not been properly inspected before the crisis. FDA officials acknowledged gaps in their ability to monitor foreign drug ingredient manufacturers, particularly as U.S. medicines increasingly relied on ingredients sourced from abroad.

Baxter recalled multiple heparin products as reports of adverse reactions mounted. Federal officials said the contaminated heparin was associated with dozens of deaths, though determining the exact number proved difficult because many patients receiving the drug were already seriously ill.

One of the most troubling questions remained unresolved: whether the contamination resulted from poor manufacturing practices or was introduced intentionally for economic reasons. Oversulfated chondroitin sulfate was cheaper than genuine heparin, leading some investigators and lawmakers to suspect deliberate adulteration. However, officials stopped short of publicly proving intent.

The scandal prompted calls for stronger testing methods, better traceability of animal-derived drug ingredients, and expanded FDA authority to inspect foreign suppliers. It also became a defining example of the risks created when critical medicines depend on long, opaque international supply chains.

**FDA Identifies Contaminant in Recalled Heparin; Says Standard Tests Failed to Detect Heparin-Like Chemical**

*Washington* — Federal health officials said a heparin-like contaminant found in recalled blood-thinning products was likely responsible for a wave of serious allergic-type reactions reported in patients across the United States, including episodes of dangerously low blood pressure and several deaths under investigation.

During a conference call, the Food and Drug Administration said the contaminant was **oversulfated chondroitin sulfate**, a chemically modified substance that closely resembles heparin in several key laboratory characteristics. Heparin is a widely used anticoagulant given to dialysis patients and others to prevent blood clots.

FDA officials said the contaminant was found in certain lots of heparin active pharmaceutical ingredient linked to adverse events. The material was associated with products distributed by **Baxter International**, which had already recalled heparin products after reports of severe reactions.

### Why routine testing missed it

Agency scientists said the contaminant evaded standard quality-control tests because it was designed or processed in a way that made it behave much like heparin. Oversulfated chondroitin sulfate carries a strong negative charge and can produce test results similar to genuine heparin under routine methods used at the time.

The FDA said existing United States Pharmacopeia tests were not sufficient to distinguish the contaminant from heparin. More advanced testing methods — including nuclear magnetic resonance and capillary electrophoresis — were needed to identify the impurity.

Officials said the finding raised concerns about weaknesses in the global supply chain for complex biologic drugs derived from animal tissue.

### Recall timeline

The heparin problem unfolded over several weeks:

- **January 2008:** Baxter began recalling certain lots of multi-dose heparin vials after reports of serious adverse reactions in patients.  
- **February 2008:** Baxter expanded the recall to include additional heparin products, eventually removing nearly all of its heparin sodium injection products from the U.S. market.  
- **March 2008:** FDA scientists announced they had identified oversulfated chondroitin sulfate as the contaminant in affected heparin supplies.

The recalled products were linked to active ingredient sourced through the international supply chain, including facilities connected to China. FDA officials said they were continuing to investigate where and how the contaminant entered the manufacturing process.

### Reported symptoms

Patients who received affected heparin reported symptoms consistent with severe hypersensitivity or anaphylactoid reactions. These included:

- Sudden drops in blood pressure  
- Shortness of breath  
- Nausea and vomiting  
- Diarrhea  
- Abdominal pain  
- Chest pain  
- Dizziness or fainting  
- Rapid swelling or flushing  

Some reactions occurred shortly after administration, particularly with higher-dose intravenous use. The FDA said it was reviewing deaths and serious injuries to determine which were directly linked to contaminated heparin.

### Company responses

Baxter said it acted quickly to recall products after becoming aware of the adverse-event reports and said it was cooperating with the FDA investigation. The company also said patient safety was its priority and that it supported expanded testing of heparin supplies.

Suppliers involved in producing the active ingredient, including firms connected to the Chinese supply chain, also faced scrutiny. Companies said they were cooperating with regulators, while FDA officials emphasized that the investigation was continuing and that responsibility for the contamination had not yet been fully determined.

The FDA said it was working with manufacturers to implement new screening methods to prevent contaminated heparin from reaching patients. Officials also said the agency was assessing the availability of alternative heparin products to avoid shortages while ensuring the safety of the drug supply.
